heading: Connect dates and the setting
intro: Start with the place you would actually visit, then consider your available dates. A description of Ecuador’s Amazon is useful background, but it cannot tell you what a particular lagoon, trail or river route will be like during your stay. Give the provider your intended arrival date, departure date and main interests. Ask how the proposed base connects those interests to the available outings. This gives you a more useful answer than choosing a month from a regional calendar and expecting every habitat to behave alike. Keep the reply with the itinerary so your group understands what was discussed before paying a deposit.
points: Name the actual destination and base.
Share your dates and wildlife interests.
Ask what those dates mean for the proposed routes.

heading: Ask about current conditions
intro: Separate the background climate from information about your departure. A description of typical rainfall is not a forecast for a particular morning, and an older travel article cannot confirm whether a route is currently operating. Ask the provider what they check before departure, what parts of the itinerary are flexible and how they communicate a change. The useful detail is the effect on your trip: a different meeting point, a changed outing or an alternative route. Record who will give you the final update and when to expect it. Avoid turning a general seasonal description into a promise about access or visibility.
points: Confirm how changes reach your group.
Keep the latest itinerary and meeting details together.

heading: Match habitats to your interests
intro: A wildlife wish list becomes more useful when you connect it to the proposed outings. Tell the guide whether your priority is birds, mammals, river life, photography or simply understanding the forest. Ask which parts of the program support those interests and how much time they allow for observation. A species mentioned in a regional guide is not a commitment that it will appear during your stay. Treat photographs as inspiration for what to learn about, rather than a checklist the guide must deliver. If your group has different interests, discuss that early so the itinerary does not revolve around one person’s preferred subject.
points: Choose a few priorities instead of a long target list.
Ask which habitats the outings visit.
Describe your group’s pace and photography needs.

heading: Discuss the guide’s daily plan
intro: Ask how the proposed day is organised rather than assuming that one hour is always best. The useful conversation connects the outing, its setting and the guide’s purpose: where the group will go, what it will look for and how long it will spend there. Explain whether early starts suit your group and whether an evening outing is something you want to consider. Confirm which activities are included and which are optional. If an outing changes, ask what the alternative would involve. This keeps the plan practical while leaving room for the guide’s judgement and the conditions encountered during the stay.
points: Connect timing to a specific outing.
Discuss early starts and evening preferences.

heading: Make time to observe
intro: Look at how the itinerary uses your time, not only how many nights you book. Arrival, departure and transfers can take up parts of a day that appear generous on a calendar. Ask how much time remains for the outings you care about, whether the schedule includes rest and how the group will move between activities. Tell the provider if you prefer a slower pace or need time to handle camera equipment. A longer stay can create more opportunities to explore, but it does not turn wildlife into an appointment. Choose a rhythm you will enjoy even when an animal you hoped to see stays out of view.
points: Identify transfer time and observation time.
Allow room for rest and your preferred pace.
Compare the actual programs, not just their night counts.

heading: Keep the final plan current
intro: Before departure, return to the details that affect your journey. Check the latest meeting arrangements, the activities in your confirmed program and the provider’s instructions for equipment. Make sure the people travelling with you have the same version of the plan. If you added a wildlife interest after booking, ask whether it fits the existing schedule rather than expecting a new outing to be included automatically. Keep current official travel advice alongside the provider’s operational information; they answer different questions. The aim is a clear, current plan with space for nature, not a calendar that promises the same experience to every traveller.
points: Share one current itinerary with the group.
Treat sightings as possibilities, never booking guarantees.
